Omitted site: tests/scripts/test_check_config_reads_heldout.py:135 `test_main_exit_codes_and_output`, whose clean case at line 144-152 builds a tree with reader `"def f(c):\n    return c.s.ghost_knob\n"` and asserts `rc2 == 0` — the section attr `s` will not match a `Config` section field named for the `.section.` receiver used by the other migrated tests.
findings.finding: The heldout-file migration inventory in AC #3 enumerates `test_unrelated_same_named_attribute_keeps_the_gate_quiet`, `test_every_real_receiver_shape_counts_as_a_read`, and the shared `_SCHEMA` fixture as edit targets, but omits `test_main_exit_codes_and_output` (tests/scripts/test_check_config_reads_heldout.py:135), which also consumes `_SCHEMA` and asserts `rc2 == 0` on the clean-path reader `c.s.ghost_knob` (line 147). That reader spells the section attribute `s`; the other migrated tests use `.section.`. Once `_SCHEMA` gains a root `Config` whose section field is named to match `.section.`, the `.s.` receiver resolves to no owner under the new owner-resolution contract, so `ghost_knob` reads as unread, `main` returns 1, and the `assert rc2 == 0` at line 151 fails.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, AC #3 ('BOTH existing gate test files are MIGRATED ...'), heldout-file bullet
scenarios: tests/scripts/test_check_config_reads_heldout.py:135 test_main_exit_codes_and_output: its clean-path `c.s.ghost_knob` receiver fails to resolve to the new section-named Config field, so main() returns 1, and `assert rc2 == 0` (line 151) fails — a broken test the migration inventory did not schedule for update.
findings.suggested_fix: Name test_main_exit_codes_and_output as a third heldout edit target and either rename the `_SCHEMA` section field to `s` (matching every receiver used across the heldout tests) or update this test's reader to `c.section.ghost_knob` so its receiver resolves to the section-owning class.

findings.finding: AC #3's test-migration inventory enumerates which tests/schema constants to migrate to the owner-resolution contract but omits test_main_exit_codes_and_output (tests/scripts/test_check_config_reads_heldout.py:135-152), whose clean-path reader `c.s.ghost_knob` (line 147) will break under owner resolution. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify the bespoke AST receiver-resolution engine against established prior art (mypy — already an installed dependency — pyright, pytype, or vulture): state explicitly why a hand-rolled cross-module fixed-point resolver is preferable to leveraging the existing type checker to resolve each attribute read's owning dataclass, per T1(b) anti-repackaging.
evidence: Plan text: 'resolve the RECEIVER expression of each ast.Attribute read to a set of candidate owning schema classes, using: the section-attribute name ... parameter/variable annotations ... local assignment propagation ... function RETURN annotations ... IfExp / BoolOp branches, and a cross-module fixed point that binds unannotated PARAMETERS from their call sites'
This is lightweight type-inference / points-to analysis — a novel architectural pattern for this repo, crossing the T1 bright-line.
resolve_symbol('mypy') -> EXISTS in site-packages; the final AC requires `make typecheck` to pass, so mypy is already a project dependency that natively knows each attribute's receiver type.

Retrieved prior art: mypy (mypy.readthedocs.io; mypy/reachability.py on GitHub), pyright (microsoft.github.io/pyright), and vulture (dead-code / unused-attribute detection) all perform receiver/type resolution or unused-symbol detection for Python.

The plan itself catalogues the resolver's 'residual permissiveness ... fail-quiet' and bare module-agnostic function-name keying — limitations a real type checker does not share — indicating a partial reimplementation of a solved problem.
findings.finding: The plan commits to a hand-rolled cross-module type/points-to inference engine (section-name resolution, annotation + local-assignment propagation, return-annotation resolution, IfExp/BoolOp branches, and 'a cross-module fixed point that binds unannotated PARAMETERS from their call sites') without considering established prior art for resolving an attribute access to its declaring type — even though a full type checker (mypy) is already an installed project dependency invoked by `make typecheck`.
findings.location: Plan section 'Design of the fix' (steps 1–3), and 'Failure direction, stated honestly'
scenarios: A newly-added config read shape the bespoke resolver cannot bind (e.g. a factory that returns a section via a helper mypy would still type) is newly FLAGGED as inert, breaking CI on a live field — the plan's own 'fail-loud' risk.
Future maintainers must extend the custom fixed-point resolver for each new receiver idiom, whereas a type checker already tracks these.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'Prior art / why bespoke' subsection to 'Design of the fix' that (1) notes mypy is already required by `make typecheck` and can resolve each `ast.Attribute` receiver's type (e.g. via `reveal_type`/dmypy or a small plugin), (2) records the concrete reasons the plan rejects it (plugin-API instability, speed, single-file scope, no new inference surface to maintain, etc.), and (3) confirms the chosen lightweight approach's fail-loud false-positive risk is acceptable given that comparison.
